answer: I'd like to talk about the only piece of jewellery I really own. A piece of jewellery that is special to me is a simple silver ring that my grandmother gave me. It originally belonged to her father, and she had kept it wrapped in a cloth in a small tin box for decades. She gave it to me when I got my first job, during one of our visits to the village, and I have treasured it ever since. It is not particularly valuable in monetary terms, but its [[sentimental]] worth is immeasurable. The ring is quite plain and old-fashioned, yet that simplicity is part of its [[charm]]. I wear it on special occasions, such as Eid, weddings and family gatherings, and doing so makes me feel closely connected to her. My grandmother has very little formal education, but she is one of the wisest people I know, and when she gave it to me, she simply said that honest work deserved something honest to wear. Every time I put it on, it brings back warm memories of that afternoon on her veranda. What makes it so meaningful is that it is a [[tangible link]] to my family's past. Honestly, it is one of my most [[cherished]] possessions, precisely because of the memories attached to it rather than its appearance. I intend to look after it carefully and one day pass it on within the family. Items like this become genuinely [[irreplaceable]], carrying stories that no new purchase ever could.

followUps.q: Do men in Bangladesh often wear jewellery?
followUps.answer: Not much, generally. A simple silver ring or a watch is quite common, but most men keep it modest. Women, on the other hand, often wear beautiful gold jewellery at weddings and festivals.
Never, no matter how much someone offered. It's not about the money at all; selling it would feel like giving away a piece of my family's history, and my grandmother would be [[heartbroken]].

note: Persona fix: grandmother is alive and gave him the ring herself (a silver ring from her father) when he got his first job; added when he wears it and her words; new mark 'tangible link'.
